d-mt.name: Dʿmt
d-mt.summary: An Ethio-Sabaean kingdom in what is now Eritrea and northern Ethiopia, likely existing from the late 8th to 6th century BCE; little is known since few inscriptions or archaeological remains survive.

land-of-punt.name: Land of Punt
land-of-punt.summary: An ancient kingdom known from Egyptian trade records for gold, resins, ebony, ivory and wild animals, likely located in the Horn of Africa; Egyptians called it 'Land of the God'.

richard-pankhurst-historian.name: Richard Pankhurst
richard-pankhurst-historian.summary: British scholar (1927–2017), a founding member of the Institute of Ethiopian Studies and professor at the University of Addis Ababa, known for research on Ethiopian economic and socio-cultural history.

ezana-of-axum.name: Ezana
ezana-of-axum.summary: Ruler of the Kingdom of Aksum from the 320s to about 360 AD who adopted Christianity and the name Ethiopia after conquering the Kingdom of Kush, having succeeded his father as a child.

axum.name: Axum
axum.summary: A town in Ethiopia's Tigray Region, once capital of the ancient Aksumite Empire, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1980 for its archaeological importance.

yeha.name: Yeha
yeha.summary: A town in northern Ethiopia's Tigray region, likely the capital of the pre-Aksumite kingdom of D'mt, known for a ruined multi-story tower dated to the 8th century BC.

kingdom-of-aksum.name: Kingdom of Aksum
kingdom-of-aksum.summary: A powerful trading kingdom in the Horn of Africa and South Arabia, founded around the 1st century, ranked among the era's four great powers, and one of the first states to adopt Christianity, in the 4th century.

sheba.name: Sheba (Saba)
sheba.summary: An ancient South Arabian kingdom in what is now Yemen, existing from around 1000–800 BCE until 275 CE, home to the Sabaean people and centered on the city of Marib.

almaqah.name: Almaqah
almaqah.summary: National moon or sun god of the pre-Islamic Sabaean kingdom of Saba in Yemen, also worshipped in Ethiopia and Eritrea.

endybis.name: Endybis
endybis.summary: Late-3rd-century ruler of the Kingdom of Aksum in East Africa, among the earliest African rulers to mint his own coins, in gold, silver and bronze.

sirwah.name: Sirwah
sirwah.summary: A city in the ancient Kingdom of Saba on the Arabian Peninsula, its capital before Ma'rib took over, and site of a temple to Almaqah built around 700 BC.

temple-of-awwam.name: Temple of Awwam
temple-of-awwam.summary: The main sanctuary of the Sabaean national god Almaqah, near ancient Marib in Yemen, active from the early 1st millennium BC to the 4th century AD; nearly a thousand inscriptions found there aid the region's history.

bar-an-temple.name: Bar'an Temple
bar-an-temple.summary: A Sabaean temple near Marib, Yemen, dating to the 10th century BCE and dedicated to the god Almaqah; also known as the "Throne of Bilqis."

dungur.name: Dungur ruins
dungur.summary: 7th-century ruins of a large structure in Axum, Ethiopia, from when the city was capital of the Kingdom of Aksum; now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gdrt.name: Gedara (GDRT)
gdrt.summary: Gadarat (GDRT): King of the Kingdom of Aksum around 200 CE, the first Aksumite king known to have involved Aksum in South Arabian affairs.

mezber.name: Mezber
mezber.summary: A pre-Aksumite archaeological site in eastern Tigray, Ethiopia, that has produced the earliest known evidence of domestic chickens in Africa.

himyar.name: Himyar
himyar.summary: A South Arabian kingdom based in the Yemeni highlands that rose to dominate most of South Arabia by the late 3rd century CE, before falling to an Aksumite invasion in the early sixth century.

mero.name: Meroë
mero.summary: An ancient city on the Nile in Sudan, capital of the Kingdom of Kush from around 590 BC until its collapse in the 4th century AD.

dbh.name: ʽDBH
dbh.summary: A king of Aksum who ruled around 230 to 240 CE, known from South Arabian inscriptions describing him aiding a Himyarite king against rival Sabaean rulers.

habesha-peoples.name: Habesha
habesha-peoples.summary: A cultural and historical identifier, also known by the exonym Abyssinians, that historically referred mainly to the Amhara, Tigrayan-Tigrinya and Gurage peoples rather than one single ethnic group.

tihamah.name: Tihamah
tihamah.summary: The Red Sea coastal plain of the Arabian Peninsula, running from the Gulf of Aqaba to the Bab el Mandeb strait.

najran.name: Najran
najran.summary: A city in southwestern Saudi Arabia, an ancient trade and agricultural center on caravan routes, notable for its pre-Islamic Christian community.

zafar-yemen.name: Zafar
zafar-yemen.summary: Ancient capital of the Himyarite kingdom in the Yemeni highlands, which at its peak (110 BCE–525 CE) ruled most of the Arabian Peninsula.

monumentum-adulitanum.name: Monumentum Adulitanum
monumentum-adulitanum.summary: A Greek inscription on a throne in Adulis describing an anonymous Aksumite king's military campaigns in Africa and Arabia, dated to about 200–270 AD, known only from a 6th-century copy.

cosmas-indicopleustes.name: Cosmas Indicopleustes
cosmas-indicopleustes.summary: A 6th-century merchant, later hermit, from Alexandria who traveled to the Kingdom of Aksum and India and wrote Christian Topography, containing some of the earliest known world maps.

lake-tana.name: Lake Tana
lake-tana.summary: Ethiopia's largest lake, in the north-western highlands, and the source of the Blue Nile.

dtwns.name: DTWNS
dtwns.summary: A king of Aksum around 272 CE, known from a Yemeni inscription recording his and his son's defeat while fighting in Arabia.

ge-ez.name: Ge'ez
ge-ez.summary: Ancient South Semitic language from Ethiopia and Eritrea, still used today as the liturgical language of Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox and Catholic churches.

ge-ez-script.name: Ge'ez script
ge-ez-script.summary: Writing system originating in Ethiopia and Eritrea, first used to write the Geʽez language and later adapted for Amharic, Tigrinya and other languages.

mani-prophet.name: Mani
mani-prophet.summary: An Iranian prophet (c. 216–274 CE) who founded Manichaeism, born near Ctesiphon in the Parthian Empire and later imprisoned and killed under the Sasanian ruler Bahram I.

manichaeism.name: Manichaeism
manichaeism.summary: A major dualistic religion founded in the 3rd century CE by the prophet Mani, teaching a cosmic struggle between light and darkness and drawing on Zoroastrian, Christian and Buddhist traditions.

orthodox-tewahedo-biblical-canon.name: Ethiopic Bible
orthodox-tewahedo-biblical-canon.summary: The 81-book biblical canon used by the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Churches, the largest and most varied biblical canon in traditional Christendom.

book-of-enoch.name: Book of Enoch
book-of-enoch.summary: An ancient Jewish apocalyptic text attributed to the patriarch Enoch, describing the origins of demons and fallen angels; it is canonical only for the Ethiopian Jewish and Orthodox traditions.

book-of-jubilees.name: Book of Jubilees
book-of-jubilees.summary: An ancient Jewish apocryphal text presenting a retelling of biblical history revealed to Moses on Mount Sinai; it survives complete only in Ge'ez translation.

ascension-of-isaiah.name: Ascension of Isaiah
ascension-of-isaiah.summary: A Judeo-Christian pseudepigraphical text dated to between 70 and 175 AD, likely compiled by an unknown Christian scribe writing as the Prophet Isaiah.

ancient-south-arabian-script.name: Ancient South Arabian script
ancient-south-arabian-script.summary: An abjad writing system used in South Arabia from the late 2nd millennium BCE to the 6th century CE, ancestor of the Ge'ez script and sibling of the Phoenician alphabet.

matara-eritrea.name: Matara
matara-eritrea.summary: A small Eritrean town and archaeological site, once a major city of the Dʿmt and Aksumite kingdoms, containing the oldest known example of Ge'ez script.

adulis.name: Adulis
adulis.summary: Ancient port city on the Red Sea, part of the Kingdom of Aksum and a hub of luxury trade with Greece and the Byzantine Empire.

abjad.name: Abjad
abjad.summary: Writing system in which only consonants are represented by letters, leaving vowels to be inferred by the reader; the term was coined by linguist Peter T. Daniels in 1990.

abugida.name: Abugida
abugida.summary: A writing system in which each symbol represents a consonant with a vowel shown by a secondary mark, unlike full alphabets or vowel-less abjads.

periplus-of-the-erythraean-sea.name: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
periplus-of-the-erythraean-sea.summary: A 1st-century Greco-Roman guide describing trade routes and ports along the Red Sea, Horn of Africa, Persian Gulf and Indian Ocean coasts.

hamadryas-baboon.name: Hamadryas baboon
hamadryas-baboon.summary: A baboon species native to the Horn of Africa and southwestern Arabia, considered a sacred animal by the ancient Egyptians.

beta-samati.name: Beta Samati
beta-samati.summary: Archaeological site near Yeha in Tigray, northern Ethiopia, an Aksumite settlement occupied from around 750 BC until the 7th century AD.

christopher-ehret.name: Christopher Ehret
christopher-ehret.summary: American scholar of African history and historical linguistics (1941–2025), a UCLA professor for nearly fifty years known for linking language reconstruction with the archaeological record.

ethio-semitic-languages.name: Ethio-Semitic languages
ethio-semitic-languages.summary: A family of Semitic languages spoken in Ethiopia, Eritrea and Sudan, including Amharic, the most widely spoken, and the liturgical language Ge'ez.

stele.name: Stele
stele.summary: A stone or wooden slab, taller than wide, erected in the ancient world as a monument, often inscribed or carved for funerary, boundary-marking, or commemorative purposes.

tigray-region.name: Tigray Region
tigray-region.summary: The northernmost regional state of Ethiopia, homeland of the Tigrayan, Irob and Kunama peoples, with Mekelle as its capital.

avalites.name: Avalites
avalites.summary: An ancient port city and trading hub in the Horn of Africa, one of the principal seaports of ancient Aethiopia, exporting ivory, tortoiseshell and high-quality myrrh.

malao.name: Malao
malao.summary: Ancient port city in present-day Somaliland, a key hub of Red Sea and Indian Ocean trade during Late Antiquity that used Roman currency.

caesarea-maritima.name: Caesarea Maritima
caesarea-maritima.summary: An ancient Mediterranean port city, capital of Roman Judaea for about 650 years, founded as a Phoenician trading village and later expanded by Herod the Great.

kingdom-of-kush.name: Kingdom of Kush
kingdom-of-kush.summary: An ancient kingdom in Nubia along the Nile in what is now Sudan and Egypt, rising from the city-state of Kerma and later ruling Egypt itself in the 8th century BCE under King Piye.

makuria.name: Makuria
makuria.summary: Medieval Nubian kingdom, capital Dongola, in what is now northern Sudan and southern Egypt; it repelled an Arab invasion in 652 and kept a resulting peace treaty for six centuries.

alodia.name: Alodia
alodia.summary: Medieval Christian kingdom in what is now central Sudan, with its capital at Soba, that thrived as a multicultural trading hub roughly from the 6th century until around 1500.

nobatia.name: Nobatia
nobatia.summary: A late antique kingdom in Lower Nubia, in what is now southern Egypt, that succeeded Kush; founded around 400, it converted to Coptic Christianity in 543 and was later annexed by Makuria.

frumentius.name: Frumentius
frumentius.summary: Phoenician missionary who became the first bishop of Aksum, converting the king and founding the Ethiopian Church in the 4th century; known locally as Abba Selama.

waaq.name: Waaqism
waaq.summary: The pre-Muslim monotheistic faith of Cushitic peoples of the Horn of Africa, centered on Waaq, the sky god, whose name still means 'God' in Oromo.

cushitic-speaking-peoples.name: Cushitic-speaking peoples
cushitic-speaking-peoples.summary: Ethnolinguistic groups who speak Cushitic languages natively, found mainly in the Horn of Africa with smaller communities in Egypt, Sudan, Kenya and Tanzania.

philip-the-evangelist.name: Philip the Evangelist
philip-the-evangelist.summary: One of the Seven chosen to care for the poor in Jerusalem in the Acts of the Apostles, who preached in Samaria and baptised an Ethiopian official.

acts-of-the-apostles.name: Acts of the Apostles
acts-of-the-apostles.summary: New Testament book recounting the early Christian Church's founding and spread across the Roman Empire, traditionally linked to Luke the Evangelist and dated to 80–90 AD.

physiologus.name: Physiologus
physiologus.summary: A didactic Christian text compiled in Greek in Alexandria describing animals and fantastic creatures with moral meanings, later translated into many languages and highly influential on medieval bestiaries and art.

tyre-lebanon.name: Tyre
tyre-lebanon.summary: Ancient Phoenician city in modern Lebanon, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world and the legendary birthplace of Carthage's founder, Dido.

arwe.name: Arwe
arwe.summary: A serpent-king in Ethiopian mythology said to have ruled for four hundred years as a tyrant demanding sacrifice, before being killed by the founder of the Solomonic dynasty.

laas-geel.name: Laas Geel
laas-geel.summary: Cave formations near Hargeisa, Somaliland, containing some of the earliest known cave paintings of domesticated cattle in the Horn of Africa, estimated at 4,500 to 5,500 years old.
